The Feedback Loop
Ep. 39: How VCs REALLY Judge Your Startup
Season 1, Ep. 40
•
Monday, November 4, 2024
How do venture capitalists REALLY think through a startup pitch? Well, today is Episode 039 of you getting to find out, as we get to hear pitches from 3 startup founders and see 2 investors react in real-time.
If you're interested in startups and founders building the future, and the venture capitalists funding them, this is a must watch. And today, we hear from founders across personalized skincare (can we finally get over all the conflicting advice on TikTok?), AI-driven nutritional tracking (our investor wants this for his gym bro son), and experiential employee benefits (can this fix our loneliness epidemic, or at least make a dent?).
It's Episode 039 of The Feedback Loop, and it's a fun one!
Pitch 1 (VAIN)
Pitch 2 (Acurixx)
Pitch 3 (ANI)
As always, hosted by Sherveen Mashayekhi, Founder & CEO of Free Agency. ​Today's guest investor, returning to the show for the FIFTH time, was Mike Ma of Sidecut Ventures.
The Feedback Loop is all about getting ambitious founders on stage to pitch and get unfiltered feedback from experienced, honest investors.
Because the thing that can hold even the best founders back from reaching their ambition? Their pitch. Whether a startup founder is raising money, recruiting a team, or selling their product, it's the pitch at the start of any given conversation that starts them on a journey to success.
For those founders on stage and in the audience, it's an answer to the essential query: how to pitch your startup.
More on our guest investor for the episode:
​​Mike is a tech CMO turned venture investor — he runs Sidecut Ventures, backing mission-driven pre-seed founders, and is an Operating Partner at Sway Ventures. He was previously MD at Nex Cubed, a pre-seed accelerator for underrepresented founders. In other words, he knows startup storytelling!
Follow Sherveen: https://x.com/Sherveen
Follow Mike: https://www.instagram.com/michaelwma
To attend The Feedback Loop in-person or apply to pitch as a founder, head to afterfeedback.com.
Thank you to all of the brave founders who participated in this episode. The Feedback Loop is dedicated to creating an engine of support for startup founders attempting to change the way the earth spins. We're on your side.
Curious as to this episode's takeaways? You'll hear about a lot, including how to think about AI features and staying competitive in the AI-driven app space, how men are stealing their girlfriends' skincare, how to sequence a startup pitch, why a question in a pitch meeting is an invitation, how to bring up your credibility as a founder, the challenges of pitching an innovative idea in a legacy industry, and so much more.
This is purpose-built for startup nerds, tech industry fanatics, future founders, and everyone in between.

But our investors question whether Mark AI’s “all‑in‑one” approach can fend off the GPT‑powered competition and keep adding value as new models improve.Why Watch?Real Pitch, Real Feedback – See how investors interrogate Daniel’s market size, competition, and product differentiation in a hotly contested AI landscape.Lessons for Founders – Learn how to distill your story into a razor‑sharp pitch, leverage personal backstory to build credibility, and define a clear go‑to‑market edge.Insight for VCs – Discover how experienced investors weigh the pros and cons of an “all‑in‑one” AI platform, and what they look for in crowded verticals like martech.--Today's guest investor was Mike MacCombie, General Partner at Generous Ventures. 74. What if AI could HAGGLE for you?
16:08| Wednesday, May 14, 2025|Season 1, Ep. 74
This startup founder wants AI to negotiate for you – whether you're buying jewelry or while you're making other high-dollar, high-stakes purchases.It’s Episode 073 of The Feedback Loop, and it's Ifeanyi Osuji pitching the future of AI driven buying.Ifeanyi's vision is an AI negotiation platform that can benchmark real‑time market prices, prompt you to ask critical questions (“How many carats is that diamond, anyway?”), and – eventually – negotiate on your behalf.But to be able to negotiate, Haggler AI needs “vertical‑by‑vertical” data – is that go-to-market approach realistic in a world where GPT‑powered solutions crop up every 7.9 seconds (don’t fact‑check that)? Our investors dig into the potential (and pitfalls) of building a B2C app for occasional high‑stakes purchases – plus the possibility of expanding into enterprise procurement, subscription cancellations, or even AI‑versus‑AI negotiations.Want to Pitch Your Startup Live?Apply now at afterfeedback.com and join our growing community of founders and investors.Follow SherveenLinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/sherveenmX (Twitter): https://www.x.com/sherveenMore on our guest investor for the episode:​Ihar Mahaniok is Managing Partner at Geek Ventures, which he founded in 2021 to support immigrant entrepreneurs building at the pre-seed and seed stage. Is Josh’s plan to integrate with OB‑GYNs realistic—or too complex?10-Year Vision vs. Immediate Traction – Investors push for a clear roadmap: focus on servicing 500 clinics first, or begin weaving in telemedicine and at‑home tech now?Josh Gottesman, founder of Embie Clinic: https://www.linkedin.com/in/josh-gottesman1Drop a comment – feedback is the building block for builders everywhere!

Friday, August 9, 2024
On the latest episode, 3 startup founders pitch their hopes and dreams, then get feedback on their storytelling + concept.
Because the thing that can hold even the best founders back from reaching their ambition? Their pitch. Whether a startup founder is raising money, recruiting a team, or selling their product, it's the pitch at the start of any given conversation that starts them on a journey to success.
As always, hosted by Sherveen Mashayekhi, Founder & CEO of Free Agency. Follow him on X at @Sherveen. Find our guest host, Mike Ma of Sidecut Ventures, on Instagram at @michaelwma.
More on Mike:
​​Mike is a tech CMO turned venture investor — he runs Sidecut Ventures, backing mission-driven pre-seed founders, and is an Operating Partner at Sway Ventures. He was previously MD at Nex Cubed, a pre-seed accelerator for underrepresented founders. In other words, he knows startup storytelling!
To attend The Feedback Loop in-person or apply to pitch as a founder, head to afterfeedback.com.

Episode Description
Mike Ma doesn’t invest in decks. He invests in people.
As Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, Mike works with what he calls “coachable superheroes”, early-stage, mission-driven founders tackling real problems in economic mobility, healthcare, climate, and education.
In this conversation, we unpack what it actually means to be coachable as a founder, why most advice fails in practice, and how real progress happens when coaching, capital, and execution collide. Mike shares lessons from the trenches — blending Fortune 500 experience with venture-backed CXO roles, and explains why the best founders don’t just seek answers, they build judgement.
We also explore Sidecut’s hands-on approach to venture building, the parallels between adaptive sports coaching and startup leadership, and why helping founders unlock potential often means meeting them exactly where they are, not where the pitch says they should be.
This episode is for founders who want fewer platitudes, better questions, and support that actually shows up.

Ep. 36: 3 Startups Pitch, 2 Investors Bicker
Season 1, Ep. 37
•
Tuesday, October 15, 2024
On Episode 036 of The Feedback Loop, we hear from founders building in: industrial automation, AI for meditation, and end-to-end encrypted AI!
As always, hosted by Sherveen Mashayekhi, Founder & CEO of Free Agency. ​Today's guest investor, returning to the show for the fourth time, was Mike Ma of Sidecut Ventures.
The Feedback Loop is all about getting ambitious founders on stage to pitch and get unfiltered feedback from experienced, honest investors.
Because the thing that can hold even the best founders back from reaching their ambition? Their pitch. Whether a startup founder is raising money, recruiting a team, or selling their product, it's the pitch at the start of any given conversation that starts them on a journey to success.
For those founders on stage and in the audience, it's an answer to the essential query: how to pitch your startup.
More on our guest investor for the episode:
​​Mike is a tech CMO turned venture investor — he runs Sidecut Ventures, backing mission-driven pre-seed founders, and is an Operating Partner at Sway Ventures. He was previously MD at Nex Cubed, a pre-seed accelerator for underrepresented founders. In other words, he knows startup storytelling!
Follow Sherveen: https://x.com/Sherveen
Follow Mike: https://www.instagram.com/michaelwma
To attend The Feedback Loop in-person or apply to pitch as a founder, head to afterfeedback.com.
Thank you to all of the brave founders who participated in this episode. The Feedback Loop is dedicated to creating an engine of support for startup founders attempting to change the way the earth spins. We're on your side.

#52: Advice Before Money: The VC Model Founders Actually Want — With Mike Ma.
Startups Decoded

Mike Ma doesn’t invest in decks. He invests in people.
As Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, Mike works with what he calls “coachable superheroes”, early-stage, mission-driven founders tackling real problems in economic mobility, healthcare, climate, and education.
In this conversation, we unpack what it actually means to be coachable as a founder, why most advice fails in practice, and how real progress happens when coaching, capital, and execution collide. Mike shares lessons from the trenches — blending Fortune 500 experience with venture-backed CXO roles, and explains why the best founders don’t just seek answers, they build judgement.
We also explore Sidecut’s hands-on approach to venture building, the parallels between adaptive sports coaching and startup leadership, and why helping founders unlock potential often means meeting them exactly where they are, not where the pitch says they should be.
This episode is for founders who want fewer platitudes, better questions, and support that actually shows up.

Ep#82: AI Was Supposed to Kill the Chief of Staff. It Made Them Indispensable. With Clara Ma
Clara Ma is CEO and Founder of Ask a Chief of Staff
Andy Walsh
Aug 17, 2026
5
2
1
Share
Transcript
AI was supposed to kill this role. Instead, it made it the most important hire you’re not making.
The big idea
Eighteen months ago, when I started this show, people had a real theory about the Chief of Staff role. AI handles the calendar, the synthesis, the meeting notes. The role gets thin, then it disappears.
The data says the opposite happened. Chief of staff postings more than doubled last year. The number of people holding the title in North America has more than tripled since 2021. Salaries at the top of the market are hitting $400K. Something is pulling in the opposite direction from what everyone predicted, and Clara Ma has been sitting inside that pull since before it had a name.
Clara was chief of staff at Hugging Face when it was still a Series A company, long before it was a household name in AI. She’s since built Ask a Chief of Staff, a 500-person community that exists because the role is still this undefined, and because nobody teaches you how to do it.
Her read on why AI grew the role instead of shrinking it: automation didn’t remove the gap between a founder’s vision and what the org actually executes. It widened it. More tools, more dashboards, more AI-generated output means more noise for a founder to filter, and someone still has to sit at the center of that noise and turn it into a decision. The takeaway for founders: the chief of staff role isn’t an assistant job that AI ate half of. It’s the translation layer AI made more necessary, not less.
The research
Chief of staff job postings more than doubled over the past year. (Revelio Labs, via Bloomberg, July 2026)
Top-of-market salaries for the role are now reaching $400,000. (Bloomberg, July 2026)
The number of people holding the title in North America has more than tripled since 2021. (Live Data Technologies)
The growth is concentrated hardest in tech and financial services, the two sectors moving fastest on AI adoption. (Live Data Technologies, via Bloomberg)
Most chiefs of staff are internal hires, because the role depends on already knowing how the organization actually gets things done. (McKinsey, via Bloomberg)
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
Subscribe
The constraint and the filter question
Every founder hits the same wall eventually. You become the bottleneck. Not because you’re bad at your job, but because you’re the only one who holds the full picture of the company in your head, and that picture has gotten too big to carry alone.
The filter question Clara uses when she’s deciding if a company is ready to hire: are you spending your time in your zone of genius, or are you spending it on synthesis and coordination? If it’s the second one, that’s the signal. Not headcount, not revenue, not stage. Just where your hours are actually going.
The framework
Clara’s framework splits the chief of staff role into two modes that show up at different company stages.
Early on, the role is almost entirely execution. There’s no one else to do the work, so the chief of staff is the one building the HR function from scratch, cleaning up the hiring process, writing the first version of processes that don’t exist yet. Clara calls this being a generalist with a spike. You cover everything, but you have one area where you go deep, and that’s usually the reason you got hired in the first place.
Later, once a company has functional leads in place, the job flips. The chief of staff stops executing on the ground and starts doing something closer to synthesis. Seeing across departments, catching the thing that’s about to become a fire before it does, deciding what actually needs to reach the CEO’s desk and what doesn’t. Clara’s phrase for it: you go from operations to people wrangler.
The failure mode is hiring for the wrong mode. A founder who needs an execution machine hires a synthesizer, or the reverse, and six months later everyone’s frustrated and nobody can explain why the hire “isn’t working out.” It’s not a skills mismatch. It’s a stage mismatch.
Education and tools
The Bloomberg reporting that sparked this episode adds useful context. Craig Stevens, managing partner at the executive search firm Boyden, told Bloomberg the complexity of the CEO role has multiplied to the point where founders can no longer sit back and think, and a chief of staff gives them that breathing space back. McKinsey’s research backs up something Clara said directly: most chiefs of staff are internal hires, because the role depends on already understanding how the organization actually gets things done, not just how it’s supposed to work on paper.
On the tooling side, Clara pointed to three things every chief of staff should have running. A note-taking tool that captures meetings automatically, so nothing depends on memory. A synthesis layer, tools like Claude or ChatGPT, that can pull context across a quarterly review, a leadership meeting, and a stack of emails to surface what actually matters. And a dictation tool like Whisper for drafting strategy docs, because typing makes people self-edit before the real thought has fully formed.
Her caution matters as much as her recommendations. AI can hand you a mountain of synthesized information. It cannot tell you what’s actually important to your CEO this quarter versus next. That judgment call is still entirely human.
“AI is a long-term memory intern. It remembers everything you tell it, but outside of that, it has no judgment. It can only follow exactly what you’ve told it, and business is still done human to human.” Clara Ma
The operating rule
The more you automate, the more valuable the one person who can turn noise into a decision becomes.

Ep#84: The Finance Skill Most Founders Never Learn
Brett Turner spent twelve years inside other people’s balance sheets before he built his own.
Andy Walsh
Sep 07, 2026
4
1
3
Share
Transcript
Most founders learn finance the hard way, in the month they run out of cash and cannot explain why.
Brett Turner learned it the other way around. Twelve years as a CPA, then a controller, then a CFO across a string of startups, some of which failed spectacularly, before he ever founded one of his own. By the time he built Trovata, his seventh company, he had already seen every version of what a cash crisis looks like from the inside.
That order matters more than people admit. Most first-time founders build the product first and back into the numbers later, treating finance as a chore they will hire their way out of eventually. Brett’s story argues the opposite. He treats cash flow, liquidity, and your own control board as the operating system running underneath the business, not a support function you delegate the moment you can afford it.
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
The data
Running out of cash is now cited as the proximate cause in up to 70% of startup post-mortems, though the root causes usually start earlier, with product-market fit and team problems doing the real damage. Review42
About 29% of startups point to running out of cash as the actual root cause, not just the trigger that finished the job. Review42
Roughly 80% of startups operate without a CFO in their early stages, meaning the numbers usually sit with a founder who never trained for the role. Embroker
A 2026 Ripple survey of over 1,000 finance leaders found 74% believe stablecoins can boost cash flow efficiency and unlock working capital currently trapped in slow settlement. StablecoinInsider
Subscribe
The workbook
Pull your last three months of bank data and compare it against your P&L. Where do they disagree, and can you explain why in one sentence.
Name the three or four numbers that actually run your business, revenue, COGS, OpEx, EBIT, whatever they are for you. Could you recite them from memory right now?
Check whether you have filed an 83(b) election if you hold founder stock. It is two pages, and it can save you real money later.
Look at your cap table like a stranger would. Does it read clean, or does it look like a decade of decisions nobody explained?
Decide honestly whether you need a full CFO, a fractional one, or just better tooling right now. Timing this wrong is expensive either way.
Big ticket items to action
Set a monthly cash review separate from your P&L review. Cash and profit tell different stories, and only one of them can bankrupt you fast.
Get your bank data and your books talking to each other automatically. Manual reconciliation is where good decisions go to die.
Build one simple cash forecast this quarter, even a rough one. A bad model beats no model every time you need to make a call fast.
“Cash tells the truth before the P&L does. Check it first.”

EP#87: Founders Obsess Over the Raise. Investors Care About This More. With Carina Cunha
Carina Cunha builds capital deals for a living. She says most founders are optimizing for the wrong finish line.
Andy Walsh
Sep 21, 2026
2
1
2
Share
Transcript
Carina Cunha is an investment banker, founder, operator, and advisor who has worked with more than 100 companies from pre-seed to IPO. She started her career in investment banking at Credit Suisse, later worked on strategy and transformation inside J.P. Morgan Private Bank alongside senior European leadership, and helped build Crimson Education into a unicorn while leading its UK and European operations.
Then she became a founder herself. Her first startup, Nosy, landed two investment offers on Dragons’ Den UK and generated more than one billion views with less than $5,000 in media spend. Today, Favikon ranks her among the Top 3 LinkedIn Voices for Sales and the Top 10 for Venture Capital.
Here’s the tension. Founders treat a raise as the win. Carina treats capital as fuel, not proof. For her, the proof is traction, and fundraising is just another sale. Capital should scale something that is already working, not fund the process of figuring out whether the theory works in the first place.
Before you can change that, she says you have to see the system you inherited. Raise big. Grow fast. Exit. Nobody chose those rules. Most founders just accept them and call it strategy.
Fact sheet
Only 63 percent of first-time VC managers who raised a debut fund go on to raise a second one, per PitchBook, despite often outperforming established firms on returns.
As many as 75 percent of venture-backed companies never return cash to their investors. Harvard Business School research covering more than 2,000 startups.
Fewer than half, 48 percent, of seed-funded startups manage to raise a follow-on round at all, according to a CB Insights analysis of over 1,100 companies.
Roughly 85 percent of startups that raise a Series A never make it to a Series B.
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
Subscribe
Carina Cunha: Building an investment bank and writing a book on human consciousness. She structures capital raises across venture, debt, and private equity, work that showed her a broken system up close. She’s advised over 100 companies from pre-seed to IPO.
The constraint
Founders inherit a system that was built by many before them. Raise big, grow fast, exit. Nobody sits you down and asks if that’s actually the outcome you want. Here’s the question to hold against your own situation. If nobody ever told you that raising was the goal, would you still be chasing this round, or would you be building the business you actually have?
The framework
Carina’s framework is capital as energy, not capital as validation. Money is fuel. It buys you time and speed, nothing more. The failure mode is treating a check as proof you’re right. It isn’t. It’s a loan against your future decisions, and every investor who writes it wants something back, whether that’s board control, a specific growth curve, or an exit on their timeline instead of yours.
Here’s the edge case that trips people up. You can take capital and still lose the operating system fight, because the money changes who you answer to before it changes what you can build. Carina’s filter for founders raising with no traction and no leverage: stop pitching a story about the market size and start being honest about what you’re actually good at and what problem you’ve actually solved, even if it’s small. Investors can smell a TAM slide that’s doing the talking instead of the founder.
The pattern underneath all five: the person across the table asking about your traction may not have any of their own. Discernment goes both ways.
Worksheet:
Before your next investor conversation, answer these honestly.
What decision have I made this month that was actually about the business, versus about what a raise would let me say?
Where is my energy leaking right now, and would more capital fix that or just fund it faster?
If this investor’s fund never raises a second one, what do they actually want from me?
What can I say about my business today, with no spin, that would still make someone want to back me? The facts!
What am I optimizing for? The round, or the company?
The operating rule
A raise is not the goal. It’s a tool, and tools only work when you know exactly what you’re building with them.

Ep#81: Where Did $18.8 Billion in AI Robot Investment Go in 2026?
John Frankel, Founder of ffVC
Andy Walsh
Aug 10, 2026
1
1
Share
Transcript
John Frankel, founder of ffVC — on where $18.8 billion in robotics money went, and why the answer isn’t the humanoid story you’d expect.
The big idea
Robotics just had its biggest funding year on record. So where did $18.8 billion actually go, and does it change anything for the rest of us.
John Frankel has been writing seed checks into physical AI since 2008, back when nobody wanted them. Farm robots, warehouse pickers, delivery drones, factory carts, he backed all of it before it was a category anyone bragged about at a dinner party. So when he maps where this year’s money landed, it’s worth following his route rather than the headline.
The number is real. Global robotics funding has hit $18.8 billion so far this year, already surpassing the $15 billion raised across all of 2025 and the $14.1 billion peak in 2021. A huge share of that is chasing humanoids, the generalized robot that can supposedly do anything. But Frankel’s own best-performing robotics bet is a company called Borough, a flatbed cart that hauls things around a farm or factory. Not glamorous. Just useful, and already deployed at scale.
The question worth sitting with isn’t whether the money is real. It’s whether it’s chasing the machine that’s actually changing anything yet, or the machine that photographs well.
Episode #81: Live now
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
Subscribe
The Data
Global robotics funding hit $18.8 billion so far in 2026, already ahead of the $15 billion invested across all of 2025 and the $14.1 billion peak from 2021. Value Add Pulse
Humanoid-specific robotics alone pulled in $8.6 billion in 2026, already 1.8 times all of 2025’s total. Briefs Finance
Tesla has logged 380,000 miles of autonomous level-four driving in the US, and only 12% of owners with the hardware actually use supervised self-driving.
Manna’s delivery drones have completed a quarter million flights, pushing delivery cost down to about a dollar versus eight to twelve dollars for a car-based delivery.
Labor now runs about 15% of production cost, down from 60 to 70% fifty years ago, and overseas labor is only about half the domestic price instead of a tenth to a twentieth.
The constraint and filter question
Here’s the friction most physical AI founders are stuck on right now. Capital wants the humanoid story because it’s the biggest possible market. But the humanoid story requires customers to trust a two hundred pound machine unsupervised in their house, and that trust doesn’t move at the speed of a fundraising round.
The filter question to hold against your own build: are you solving a problem people will let into their home or factory unsupervised today, or are you betting on a comfort curve that might take a decade longer than your cap table can survive?
The framework
Frankel’s mental model has two separate curves, and most people only track one of them.
The first is the technology curve. This one moves in leaps you can’t schedule. He compared it to inventing something new: put in a certain amount of capital or intellectual effort, and you might get a breakthrough tomorrow, or in a hundred years. Nobody controls the timing.
The second is the adoption curve, and this one is almost always slower and more predictable than founders want it to be. His proof point is blunt. Tesla has logged 380,000 miles of autonomous level-four driving in the US. The technology, by his own admission, surprised him. But only 12% of Tesla owners with the hardware actually use supervised self-driving. Eighty-eight percent sit on capability they don’t touch. People who don’t own a Tesla insist their car already does this. It doesn’t. The belief curve and the capability curve aren’t even the same shape.
Apply that to robots in a home. It’s one thing to watch a robot wash dishes while you supervise. It’s another to trust it unsupervised near a kid, a dog, or anything breakable. Frankel thinks factories solve first, because factories are constrained environments where you can control variables a living room never will. Homes are a comfort problem before they’re a capability problem, and comfort takes years nobody’s cap table is built to survive.
The failure mode he’s watching for is founders who build for the technology curve and price their business for the adoption curve to match. It won’t. The businesses working right now, Manna’s drone deliveries, Borough’s farm and factory carts, plus one robotics in package sorting, all picked a narrow job with obvious ROI and no home-comfort problem to solve. They didn’t wait for the humanoid dream. They shipped the boring version first.
Education and tools
The funding data backs up the split Frankel is describing. Humanoid-specific robotics startups alone have raised $8.6 billion in 2026, already 1.8 times all of 2025, with names like Figure AI and Neura Robotics pulling nine-figure and ten-figure rounds. That’s capital betting hard on the generalized robot story Frankel is skeptical of. Meanwhile the categories actually generating revenue today, warehouse and logistics automation, agricultural robotics, delivery, are less headline-grabbing and better proof that Frankel’s point solution thesis is playing out in real deployment numbers, not just funding totals.
His reshoring point is worth the same scrutiny. Fifty years ago labor was 60 to 70% of production cost, and overseas labor was a tenth to a twentieth the price. Today labor is closer to 15% of cost and only about half the price overseas. The economics that justified offshoring in the first place have mostly evaporated, which is a big part of why he expects a wave of US-based physical AI companies to have a real structural advantage over the next decade.
“A company that makes sense in January is dumb as shit in March.” John Frankel
The operating rule
Build for the adoption curve you can prove today, not the technology curve you’re hoping shows up.

Most founders are making their hardest decisions alone. Nobody is there when the decision is genuinely hard. If you want unfiltered truth from 2 exits and $10M ARR, email me.

To the Editor: 
For the past 34 years, men’s Division 11 basketball has had championship 
play with a field of 32 teams selected for the competition. In recent years 
(since 1984) 12 to I5 teams have been automatic qualifiers through their 
conferences, with the remaining teams selected as at-large teams. Having 
served on the NCAA Division II Basketball Committee for six years (1983 
to 1989), I have witnessed anywhere from eight to 12 teams each year with 
outstanding records of ZO-plus wins that are not selected. 
It is time to expand the NCAA championship for men’s Division II 
basketball to, preferably, 48 teams, for many good reasons. 
A. Men’s NCAA Division II Basketball always shows a net profit and 
has since the beginning of college-division basketball in 1957. 
B. A number of good teams normally not selected would have the 
opportunity to compete in NCAA championship play. 
C. NCAA Division II membership has increased by 28 schools in the 
past 11 years. In 1980, there were 178 Division 11 members playing men’s 
basketball; in 1991, there were 206 Division II members playing men’s 
basketball. 
D. As membership increases, opportunity to be selected as an at-large 
team diminishes. 
E. An expanded field of teams would allow thousands of additional fans 
to see high-caliber championship competition. 
Charles G. Smith 
Director of Athletics 
University of Missouri, St. Louis

Lady Vols Tennessee coach Pat Summitt 
admonished her team to play with 
its heart and its head in the Division 
I Women’s Basketball Champion- 
ship’s title game against Virginia 
March 3 I in New Orleans. And one 
Head- junior Dena Head-was 
the critical factor in the Lady Vols’ 
70-67 overtime victory. 
Head set a championship-game 
record with 28 points (which was 
matched by Virginia’s Dawn Staley), 
made critical free throws at the end 
of regulation and in overtime, and 
made a key defensive play on Virgi- 
nia’s last possession in regulation. 
“The free throws at the end of 
regulation were key to make, and I 
knew that,” Head said of the shots 
that knotted the score at 60 and sent 
the title contest into overtime for 
the first time in this championship’s 
history. “When Daedra (Charles) 
went out of the game (fouled out), I 
told her I’d make them for her.” 
Virginia had one more opportu- 
nity in regulation. StaIey took the 
triumph in overtime inbounds pass and went the length 
of the court, but Head got a hand 
on the shot. 
“Dena Head did a great defensive 
job on the last shot; she blocked it,” 
Staley said. “It was a great defensive 
play.” 
“Dawn Staley is a great player, 
and I was glad I got a piece of the 
ball in the play at the end of regula- 
tion,” Head said. “She could have 
easily won it for her team.” 
The title game was a rematch of 
last year’s East regional champion- 
ship game, in which Virginia de- 
feated Tennessee in overtime to 
reach the Women’s Final Four for 
the first time. 
“Last year, losing to Virginia in 
the tournament really hurt us,“Sum- 
mitt said. “We were upset losing to 
them in overtime and not having 
the opportunity to be in the Final 
Four on our home court and in 
front of our home fans. 
“(This) win feels like the greatest 
of all the national championships,”

Northern Michigan forward

utes and 57 seconds, Northern Mich- 
igan won its first national cham- 
pionship and finished the season 38- 
54. 
“It would have been terrific to 
win it and be called national cham- 
pions, but we had a nice ride,” said 
Boston U. coach Jack Parker. “It 
wasn’t just a hockey game. We 
created something different tonight.” 
They created momentum swings 
that bordered on the bizarre. Boston 
U. led, 3-0, after the first period and 
looked like the fresher team. 
“If they had gotten to 4-0, we 
would have been in trouble,” said 
Northern Michigan coach Rick 
Comley, whose team went unde- 
feated the last 26 games (24-O-2) of 
the season. 
At the intermission, the Wildcats 
knew they would start the second 
period in a man-up situation after 
Peter Ahola took a high-sticking 
penalty at the 20-minute mark. 
Added Comley, “I was close to 
panic. But I did believe that if we 
got the next goal we would be right 
back in it.” 
At 1:33 of the second period, 
Dean Antos opened the floodgates 
and hit a backhander to get the 
Wildcats on the board. What ensued 
shocked all of the 12,564 in attend- 
ance. Northern Michigan reeled off 
another five straight goals, including 
three by the nation’s leading scorer, 
Scott Beattie, to take what seemed 
to be a commanding 6-3 lead with 
16:52 left in regulation. 
“We played so well in the second 
period, maybe better than we’ve 
ever played,” said Comley. 
Plandowski, who also had a hat 
trick, scored the second of his three 
goals on a power play at 824 of the 
third period and the Wildcats 
seemed in control at 74.

Emma wins IioDev BaKer David Emma, a senior forward 
for Boston College’s ice hockey 
team and the school’s career scoring 
leader, is this year’s Hobcy Baker 
Memorial Award winner as the 
outstanding player in the sport. 
The announcement of Emma’s 
selection was made March 30 at the 
St. Paul Civic Center in St. Paul, 
Minnesota, site of the Division I 
Men’s ICC Hockey Championship. 
Emma finished his career with a 
school-record 239 points in 145 
games. He also set school records 
for most career assists (127) and 
most career goals (112). 
The 1991 Hockey East Associa- 
tion player of the year, Emma aver- 
aged 2.25 points per game, which 
ranked fourth in the country. He 
also is one of only two players in 
Boston College history to score 80 
or more points in one season and 70 
or more points twice in a career. 
“David approaches his academics 
and hockey as he does his life- 
totally committed both physically 
and mentally,” said Boston College 
coach Len Ceglarski. “He has a 
purpose in everything he does and is 
not satisfied until his goal is reached. 
On the ice, he does all the little 
things that make for a great player.

sual intensity every shift on the ice.”

Minnesota program receives two-year probation I. Intmductlon. 
In March 1988, the NCAA Committee 
on Infractions issued a report that found 
that the University of Mmncsota, Twin 
Cities, had violated NCAA rules concern- 
ing extra benefits to enrolled studcnt- 
athletes and other NCAA rules in the 
operation of the university’s men’s has- 
ketball program. There were numerous 
violations that spanned the period 1982 10 
1986. Although there also were limited 
violations in the football program, the 
committee noted that the violations in the 
men’s basketball program were *serious 
in nature,*’ and “many occurred because 
the men’s basketball coaching staff chd 
not seek guidance concerning rules inter- 
pretations” Among the violations found 
was a violation of the principles of institu- 
tional control. The March 1988 infractions 
report stated: 
“Over a substantial period of time, 
there were repeated failures to exercise 
adequate institutional control over the 
administration of the university’s men’s 
mtercollegiate athletics program. In addi- 
tion to the findings set forth previously in 
this report, this failure of institutional 
control was demonstrated by: administra- 
tive procedures that allowed student- 
athletes lo receive prepaid airline rickets; 
the provision of mileage expense money 
to the student hosts for prospective slum 
dent-athletes during official visits; the 
disbursement of ‘meal money’ and other 
very small amounts of cash in a manner 
that may have constituted rules violations; 
the provision of meals 10 more than one 
student-athlete who dined with a pro- 
spective student-athlete during the pros- 
pect’s official visit in a manner that 
violated NCAA legislation, inadequate 
administrative procedures lo ensure that 
linancial aid given 10 student-athletes in a 
school year following the completion 01 
their competitive eligibility was m con- 
formance with NCAA legislation. (NCAA 
Constitution 3-2)” 
The committee also found in 1988 that 
the pen&es imposed on the university 
for its violations should be mitigated 
because of “the thoroughness of the uni& 
versity’s self-investigation, its cooperation 
in the NCAA investigation and its correc- 
tlve actions (including taking dlsciphnary 
action against the involved coaches and 
the creation of a comprehensive com- 
pliance program).” 
However, one month after the commir- 
tee’s report in 1988, the university unto- 
vered informatIon during the course of an 
audit of its Office of Minority and Special 
Student Affairs (OMSSA) indicating that 
the then director of the program had 
misappropriated university funds totaling 
at least Sl86,000. The director claImed 
the majority of these funds had been 
given to student-athletes as financial as- 
sistance. This director briefly had served 
as an academic adviser m 1984 to the 
football team and in 1986 to the men’s 
basketball team, and he had extensive 
contact wirh student-athletes during tus 
assignments with OMSSA. An invest&- 
tlon was launched by the university that 
evenrually involved local law enforcement 
authorities. In November 1989, the former 
director was convicted on three coums of 
theft by swindle and has since served a 
term of imprisonment for these offenses. 
During the course of rhe investigation 
of the actlvlties of the former director of 
OMSSA, additional allegations of viola- 
tions surfaced involving Ihe university’s 
men’s basketball, football and wrestling 
programs. The university discovered and 
self-reported a number of these violarions 
in the course of its own audits of its 
athletics program, which were m&ted as 
part of the university’s new comphance 
program. 
By the time the university and NCAA 
enforcement staff concluded their inquir- 
ies, it became evident that the extent to 
which funds misappropriated from the 
university had been diverted for the benefit 
of student-athletes was substantial, but 
significantly less than the former director 
had claimed. As reflected in the findings 
in this case, approximately 63,700 was 
provided to student-athletes from the 
OMSSA special loan account (reference: 
Part II-A of this report); approximately 
166,700 in benefits was provided to IO 
student-athletes out of a total of $44,000 
in 268 transactlons thTough the manipu- 
latlon of journal voucher payments (ref- 
erence: Part II-B of this report), and there 
was at least 69,000 in other loans and 
payments to student-arhleres hy the 
former director of OMSSA (reference 
Part II-C of this report). 
‘The violations in this case, m&ding 
those where the rhen director of OMSSA 
was involved, primarily concerned the 
unrverslty’s football program. The viola- 
tions occurred, for the most part, prior to 
the university’s March 1988 case. Al- 
though the improper benefits the director 
of OMSSA gave student-athletes began 
as early as 1982, there was a pattern of 
violations from 1982 until their discovery 
in April 1988. In the committee’s view, the 
university’s failure to supervise and control 
rhe activities of the involved director of 
OMSSA relating to student-athletes dur- 
ing this period of time demonstrates a 
failure of institutional control over the 
conduct of the institution’s intercollegiate 
athletics program. Although there was no 
evidence that any other university admin- 
istrator knew of or authorized the actions 
of the director of OMSSA, the university 
agreed there were signals that the univer- 
sity did not detect rhat probably would 
have led to an earlier disclosure of the 
unauthorized actions. As a result, the 
director of OMSSA was able to pursue an 
independent agenda using university rem 
sources for a considerable period of time. 
That agenda, it turned out, involved 
many more students who were not athletes 
than students who were. Nonetheless, 
these actions dragged the university’s 
athletics program into significant viola- 
tions of NCAA rules concerning extra 
benefits and financial aid to student- 
athletes. To the uruversity’s credit, the 
university’s own audit systems eventually 
led IO the uncovering of these problems. 
Once the university became aware of 
them, it acted swiftly to remove the direc- 
tar of OMSSA from the institution and 
brought the matters to the attention of 
law enforcement agencies for investigation 
and prosecution. 
The Committee on Infractions regarded 
the cluster of findings of violations in- 
volving the director of OMSSA as major 
in nature(reference: Paris II-A, II-B, 11-C 
and II-D of this report). Most of the 
student-athlete recipients of these benefits 
were football players. A total of 23 foot- 
ball student-athletes from 1983 through 
1988 were involved. Although there were 
reasons to mitigate some of the penalties, 
as discussed subsequently, the NCAA 
required minimum penalties for major 
rules violations were applicable to the 
university’s foothall team because of these 
viola~lonr. 
The football program also violated the 
rules specifying the minimum academic 
requirements for graduate assistant 
coaches (reference: Part II-E of this re- 
port). These violations gave the football 
program a competitive advantage over a 
three-year period because it gave the 
program the services 01 a large number of 
extra coaches that ir was not entitled to 
use. Although the committee did not have 
Lo decide if this violation standing alone 
would constitute a major violation in light 
of the committee’s conclusion that the 
other violations made the major violator 
penalties applicable, the committee be- 
lieved this was a significant set of viola- 
tions that contmued through the 1989-90 
academic year. 
The violations involving the uruverslty’s

Owen's brand new book, Internal Propaganda, is out now!
Andy Walsh

Transcript
The Voice In Your Head Is Not Yours. It Just Sounds Like It Is.
You think you reasoned your way into that decision. The raise, the hire, the pivot. You didn’t. Something in you decided first, and your brain spent the next hour building a case for it.
Owen Fitzpatrick has spent thirty years trying to figure out why. He interviewed people inside North Korea, Rwanda, and Afghanistan to study how belief actually forms, then spent two decades applying it with leaders at Google, Pfizer, and LinkedIn. His new book is called Inner Propaganda, and the argument is simple. The most dangerous propaganda in your life isn’t coming from outside. Your own brain is running it, all day, without asking permission.
Full episode with Owen Fitzpatrick is live now.
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
Subscribe
The numbers, before we go further
CB Insights studied 431 failed VC-backed startups in 2024. 43% died from poor product-market fit. Not a cash problem. A belief that felt right long enough that nobody stopped to check if it still made sense.
Those same companies raised $17.5 billion combined before shutting down. Median raise: $11 million. Money bought time for the story to keep running, not evidence that the story was true.
Median time from last raise to shutdown: 22 months. A quarter stayed “walking dead” three-plus years. That’s not slow data. That’s a belief that had already passed Fitzpatrick’s first two gates, feels right and fits identity, doing everything it could to survive the third.
Naming a feeling with precision, not just “stressed” but the exact word, measurably lowers activity in the brain’s threat response. Get specific before the feeling picks your story for you.
Hold those in mind. Now the story.
Presented by Deel. If you’re making your first or fiftieth hire — and doing it across borders — Deel is worth knowing. They’re supporting Startups Decoded. LEARN MORE.
The pause that stopped a nuclear war
In 1983, a Soviet engineer named Stanislav Petrov sat in front of an alarm system reporting five incoming American missiles. Protocol said report it up the chain. Command would have retaliated.
Petrov paused. He asked himself one question: does this make sense. Five missiles wasn’t a real first strike, it was a fraction of what an actual attack would send. He was right. The alarm was a false read caused by light hitting cloud cover. He is, by most honest accounts, the reason there was no nuclear war that day.
The training that saved millions of lives wasn’t confidence. It was the habit of asking what would have to be true for this to be false before acting on it.
Why your brain skips that step
Fitzpatrick’s framework for how a belief takes hold runs in a specific order, and it’s not the order you think. A belief has to feel right first. Then it has to fit who you think you are. Only after both of those boxes are checked does your brain go looking for reasons it makes sense.
Logic is the last gate, not the first. This is why you can know a decision is a mistake and make it anyway. The belief that felt right and matched your identity as a founder got there before the knowledge did, and it’s still steering.
Fitzpatrick calls it inner propaganda for a reason. Propaganda doesn’t ask you to evaluate it. It asks you to feel it, then belong to it. Your own brain runs the same playbook on you every single day, and you’re the only audience it needs to convince.
Where it actually costs you
Runway pressure is the perfect breeding ground for this. You’re not sure the plan is working, the doubt creeps in, and your brain needs a story fast because uncertainty is expensive to sit in.
So it hands you one. A real founder would have closed by now. A real founder wouldn’t still be figuring this out. None of that is evidence. It’s a story built to make the discomfort of not knowing go away, and it will cost you a decision you’d have made differently with a clear head.
The filter you actually need
Fitzpatrick’s fix isn’t more information, it’s a different question. Stop asking where’s my evidence for this, because your brain will always find some. Ask instead whether the belief is actually serving you. That question can’t be answered with confirmation bias. It forces you to look at outcomes instead of conviction.
Pair it with a number. Poker player and author Annie Duke has a test worth using: attach a percentage to how sure you are before you act, zero to a hundred. Say it out loud. Most founders find their certainty drops fast once there’s an actual number attached to it.
The workbook
Run this before your next big call.
Name the belief driving the decision. Write the actual sentence, not the polished version. “A real founder would have closed by now” counts.
Put a number on it. Zero to a hundred, how sure are you? If you wouldn’t bet real money on that number, don’t act on the belief yet.
Ask what would have to be true for the opposite to be correct. This is the Petrov question. It surfaces the case you’ve been avoiding.
Separate the belief from the evidence. Write down what actually happened this week, no interpretation. Then write the story you told yourself about it. See how far apart they are.
Audit it after the fact. When the decision plays out, go back and check whether the belief that drove it held up. Patterns show up fast once you start tracking this.
The belief that feels most true under pressure is usually the one that’s had the least scrutiny. Test it before you trust it.
“No matter how true it feels, what you’re going through right now is a lie.”
The takeaway
Before you act on conviction, ask what would need to be true for you to be wrong.

Ep#83: How To Find New And Unexpected Customers. With Bryan Alston
Why you are missing vital customer data
Andy Walsh
Aug 24, 2026
3
1
Share
Transcript
Most founders think they know their customer. They’ve got a loose ICP written down somewhere. Age, income, job title, maybe a quote about their pain point.
What they don’t have is the why.
Why this person bought, what they almost bought instead, what tipped them over the edge at 11pm on a Tuesday. That gap between who you think you’re selling to and why they actually buy is where the growth is hiding, and almost nobody goes looking for it.
Bryan Alston has spent fifteen years as what he calls a marketing detective, working with brands like Magic Spoon, Our Place, Clove and Best Day Brewing. His job isn’t finding more data. It’s finding the customer everyone else ignored.
What the research says:
Segmented campaigns can lift revenue by up to 760%. Market Force
Personalization drives 5 to 15% revenue growth, per McKinsey. HubSpot
Word of mouth decides 20 to 50% of purchase decisions, especially first-time buys. arxiv
Tight, trusted networks carry less reach but far more impact than public feeds. arxiv
Last-click models undercount channels like email and referrals, the ones founders cut first. Osmos
None of that is a coincidence. It’s the mechanism behind everything Bryan describes.
The story that anchors this episode is Greater Than, a sports hydration brand Bryan ran as CMO. It launched for athletes, priced at eight dollars a bottle against Gatorade’s two or three. Then random spikes of traffic they couldn’t trace. Then the comments filled with photos of breast milk. A wave of breastfeeding mothers had found the drink solved their fatigue and low milk supply, and they were tagging ten friends each in private groups. Greater Than leaned in. Three years later, three hundred thousand dollars a year had become ten million, profitably.
The constraint.
Founders optimize the customer they already have instead of asking who else has this exact problem. It feels safer. It’s also how you end up bidding against a bigger competitor for their leftover customers.
The framework.
Bryan’s method starts by asking what the product actually does, not what category it’s sold in. A sports drink is really an electrolyte solution with no added sugar. Reframe it and your customer pool opens up.
The trap is chasing the incumbent’s audience instead, what Bryan calls paying for their table scraps.
The other trap is measurement. Attribution windows built for seven-day wins quietly kill anything whose payoff takes longer, so find your product’s real latency and measure against that instead.
“If you try to copy your biggest competitor, you’re not just overpaying for their table scraps. You’re making them more money too.” Bryan Alston
The workbook
Pull up your own numbers and answer these before you do anything else this week.
Write down what your product actually does, stripped of category language. Not “we sell X,” but the underlying job it performs.
List every customer group who has that exact underlying problem, even ones who’d never buy from your category today.
Pull your last 20 support tickets, reviews or DMs. Flag anything mentioning a use case, a life stage, or a reason you didn’t expect.
Calculate your real latency: average days between someone’s first touch and their first purchase. If you don’t know it, that’s this week’s job.
Pick one overlooked group from step 2. Name the smallest possible test you could run against it for under $500.

Ep #84: Why Most Founders Get Their Angel Round Wrong. With Vadim Gordin.
Fresh research on the way to close an angel round.
Andy Walsh
Aug 31, 2026
3
2
1
Share
Transcript
Most founders think they’ve done the work once they’ve built a pitch deck and a list of names.
What they haven’t done is the math. How many conversations does one check actually take? How long does the whole thing really run? What does a messy early cap table cost you two years from now, quietly, when nobody’s looking?
Vadim Gordin (Healing Healthtech) has spent years closing that gap. He ran a venture studio inside NYU Tandon that helped 300 teams raise $2.7 billion, then built a custom dataset of first-person fundraising accounts to answer the question nobody else was tracking: not who got funded, but what it actually took to get there.
What the research says:
Warm intros convert at 8 to 12% from intro to meeting. Cold emails convert at 2 to 4%. DocSend, via The VC Wire
The median time to close a seed round hit 142 days in 2025, more than double the 68 days it took in 2021. Carta, via HummingDeck
About 18.5% of US households meet the SEC’s accredited investor test. Only a small fraction of those ever write an angel check. Walnut
Roughly one in four companies that pitch angels actually get funded. Walnut, citing UNH Center for Venture Research
Angels provide close to 80% of outside equity for early stage startups, more capital sources than most first time founders ever think to tap. Center for Venture Research / NVCA
None of that is random. It’s the mechanism behind everything Vadim describes.
The story that anchors this episode isn’t a single company, it’s a pattern Vadim kept seeing across hundreds of raises. Founders would land twenty real conversations and walk away with one or two checks, every time, regardless of industry. They’d treat that ratio like a personal failure. It’s not. It’s just the shape of the funnel. Vadim built his entire coaching practice, an 80% follow-on funding rate at his last NYU cohort, around teaching founders to trust that math instead of panicking inside it.
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
Subscribe
The constraint.
Founders treat the friends and family round like a warm up. A box to check before the real fundraise starts. Vadim’s data says that’s backwards. The habits you build raising your first dollars, how you track conversations, how you manage expectations with people who love you, are the same habits that will make or break your Series A cap table two years later.
The framework.
Vadim calls it the traction funnel. The idea is simple: every relationship with a future investor moves through a stack of increasing commitments. A stranger agrees to a conversation. Then they share information. Then they run a small pilot. Then they sign something real. Each step earns you the right to ask for the next one.
The trap most founders fall into is skipping straight to the ask. They want a check before they’ve earned a conversation, let alone a pilot.
The other trap is pacing. Vadim contrasts the marathon fundraise, an exhausting, open ended drip of asks, with the sprint, where founders lock in a follow up meeting before they leave the first one, build urgency with real traction updates, and close a tight window on purpose.
“Nobody who could have raised an angel round should fail to do so if we give them adequate information.” Vadim Gordin
The workbook
Pull up your own numbers and answer these before your next investor conversation.
Count your last twenty investor conversations. How many turned into a second meeting, and how many of those turned into a check.
Are you running a sprint or a marathon right now, and did you actually choose that, or did it just happen to you.
List your last five investor intros. How many came from someone who has actually written a check into that person’s portfolio.
Write down your guardrail number, the dollar amount and time horizon you and your household have agreed on before this raise puts real strain on your life.
Pick one gap in your process, meeting conversion, check conversion, or intro quality, and name the smallest fix you could test in the next two weeks.
Listen: Apple || Spotify || YouTube

July  2018 
VISIT OUR WEBSITE at SV ASociety.org and visit us on Facebook 
Watch Pam’s Videos of SV AS meetings on YouTube at: accordionpam 
SV AS  Next  Meeting:  
Sunday , August 5 at Harry’s Hofbrau 
There IS a Jam Band session in Aug.  Vic and Barbara Corsiglia will lead the session from ap-
proximately 1:15 until 1:50.  Then it is open mike from 2:00 to 2:30.  Contact Pam for a time 
slot.  Pick at least one piece, get it/them ready, and let a very sympathetic audience listen.   
Nothing to lose! 
 
Il Duetto Musica is a delightful mix of Opera & Popular Italian Street Songs featuring the talents of soprano Gloria 
Mendieta Gazave and accordionist Paul Aebersold. 
Enjoy a nostalgic tribute to the charm of Italy as you 
listen to such favorites as Arrivaderci Roma and 
Puccini classics from La Bohéme and other great 
operas. Gloria & Paul take you on a Gondola ride 
through Venice with romantic songs, lively music, 
and colorful costumes for an evening of musical 
treasures.  
 
Gloria Mendieta Gazave is a classically trained so-
prano from San Francisco, CA with a background in 
Musical Theater.  She was selected to sing for Pope 
John-Paul II. Ms. Gazave sings in Italian, French, 
German, and Spanish. 
 
Paul Aebersold realized his love for music as a child 
listening to his mother play the accordion. He has 
performed for several years on the East Coast. Mr. 
Aebersold was honored to perform for the French 
Embassy in Washington D.C. He has recently moved to Redwood City and is enjoying his collaboration of Italian 
Street Songs and Opera arias with soprano Gloria Mendieta Gazave.  


                       
   SILICON VALLEY ACCORDION SOCIETY              JULY 2018                        Page  2 
Did you miss a meeting performance?  You can view some of it on YouTube. To view Pam’s Videos from past 
meetings: Go to youtube.com, type in “accordionpam” in the search field  
(next to the magnifying glass on top) for videos from the club . 
President’s Message 
 
Summer is definitely upon us, and we started it off with a Big Bang! Nothing like Mike Marotta's 
"Monterey International" group to get everyone's "juices flowin". And it was great to see and 
hear Rudy Pivk playing us some fabulous music on his beautiful Hohner Gola accordion. A beauti-
ful combination! And a lot more! See Marybarbara's write-up. And Marybarbara, it was nice to 
see you looking so well!! 
 
A special thanks to Pam Kawashima for all of her hard work scheduling our performers. This is 
a MAJOR job--time consuming and often frustrating! AND, she is also our Web-Meister and keeps 
our web-site humming! And this includes being the videographer of our performers! Pam is a most 
important member of our organization, and her work is greatly appreciated. THANK YOU, PAM! 
 
Did you notice that Steve Hansen (the Bass-player) had his right foot in a soft cast? (He injured it 
helping a neighbor) Well, Steve says that this situation turned into a learning experience for him and allowed him to add 
some versatility to his musicality. He usually played his cymbals with his right foot. This injury forced him to learn to play 
with his left foot. This in turn allowed him to add some additional options, in that he could use his left hand tapping the 
cymbals, and still have his right hand free to use the bow! Innovative! Steve is a much sought-after addition to many music 
groups!   
 
And, our very own Scott Stanfield was invited by Mike Marotta to play his drums/bongos during a latin number! And, he 
did extremely well! Way to go, Scott! 
 
We have a new Mascot: his name (a compilation of suggestions submitted by the audience) is "Little Harry (Hairy!) 
MORGANI"! Harry was donated to the SVAS by Barbara Winter. Thanks, Barbara, and thanks to all the folks who 
submitted suggestions for his new name! 
 
Our sincere condolences go out to the family and friends of Lucille Basso, who died recently. Lucille was a long-time regu-
lar attendee at our concerts, and we shall miss her.  We are also aware that several of our members are struggling with vari-
ous health challenges. We sincerely wish them well, and rapid healing! 
 
We are looking for a "Tex-Mex" accordion player/combo. Anyone have any suggestions? 
 
My "Parting Shot" for this month is this: Have you ever seen yourself playing your instrument on video? When I was a 
training coordinator, both Military and civilian, we video-taped instructors' rehearsals and deliveries, followed by critiques. 
Well, I recently had the Frustrating (!) experience of seeing myself playing a selection on YouTube (Thanks, 
Pam!!)  BAD! So, if you have the opportunity to video-tape yourself playing, do so. You might learn a thing or two!! 
 
That's all for now. Please stay safe and well. We hope to see you next month! 
Bill, President Again. 
Bill Tapogna 
Marybarbara was our Reporter for this month.  You can read her report starting on page 4.  
Marybarbara is very organized when it comes to the report.  You can see how she set up her 
“home office” with laptop and mobile desk to capture the report.   
 
 
 Lou and Karen Buonomo ran the admis-
sions desk at the meeting.  Lou is also one 
of the stalwart crew who set up the room 
and sound system before the meeting 
starts. 


Silicon Valley Accordion Society                          JULY 2018                          Page 3 


  
 SILICON VALLEY ACCORDION SOCIETY             JULY      2018                          Page  4 
In our fast-paced Silicon Valley world where an ADHD (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) ex-
istence is the expected norm, not the exception, how do we step back and try to relax and rejuvenate 
our own lives?   Can we even find the time to do this? Summertime, especially in northern California, 
can offer us the perfect opportunity!  
The first Sunday of each month offers us a perfect opportunity to take time away from our desks, not 
to mention our electronic devices, and to feel the healing effects of great music and moments of cama-
raderie from fellow lovers of accordion music.  Which brings me to the naked ladies! Also known as 
Amaryllis belladona, they are wild lilies, whose strikingly pink blossoms with leafless stalks seem to 
pop out of nowhere along California roadsides during the summer months.  Although there were no 
naked ladies at our July 8 meeting there was plenty to surprise and delight us.  Take this past Sunday 
for example. 
Sue Douglas kicked us off with a medley of summertime songs including 
Featherlight Waltz (a tune she composed herself),  You are my Sunshine, Red, 
Red Robin, and Mexican Hat Dance which naturally reminded me of Mexican 
jumping beans.  Speaking of beans. . .  
Plant a bean seed and it will almost certainly grow and pro-
duce a generous harvest.  Don Savant’s performance treat-
ed us to a generous and healthy dose of easy listening jazzy 
numbers.  Doesn’t Don have his own unique style of synco-
pation and rhythmic chordal accompaniments, all charac-
teristics of great jazz?  His rendition of Nature Boy fit right into the summer gar-
den theme.  We paid no attention to Don when he played Do Nothing Til You 
Hear from Me.  Our assembled crowd then broke into appreciative applause.  
Luckily we haven’t had much Stormy Weather but we all agreed that indeed we 
live in a Wonderful World. 
 
It is indeed a 
wonderful 
world, espe-
cially when 
Sunday Sev-
en entertains 
us with their 
well rehearsed 
numbers.  
Opening up 
with several 
German tunes 
we quickly 
moved to the Alpine region of Switzerland with, what else, Alpine Polka!  Now you might think that 
at such high elevation gardens would be difficult to cultivate.  Au contraire! Carrots are a particular 
favorite of Swiss gardeners. Although United States gardening conditions may be very different from 
the Swiss Alps, we both share the same national pride and the ideology of love and devotion to home-
land.  America the Beautiful, featured a lovely solo by recorder player, Gloria Tapogna.  Of course, 
July wouldn’t be complete at Harry’s without God Bless America and the tunes included in the Armed

out of your own backyard garden. . . except possibly  when you’re in the audience at Harry’s Hofbrau

this month, so if you haven’t sent in your check, this is a good time to take a few minutes and send us your membership 
We do not talk in a monotone – but rather with changes in pitch, speed, and volume.  
Our music should be the same!  Rudy Pivk, is well aware and has mastered the skill of 
combining right hand technique and bellows.  Playing a selection of well known jazz 
and pop songs that included the bolero mambo, Sway and Rocco Granata’s signature 
song, Marina, Rudi’s skill demonstrated that our hands play the notes and the bellows 
give them shape.  Rudi finished his set with the ever-popular, Jalisco.   
 
We were treated to an unex-
pected bonus when Diane Salmon, played her 19 
pound green sparkly Serenellini accordion that orig-
inally belonged to Mike Marotta senior.  Diane was 
a student of Mike Marotta several years ago and 
recently returned to studying with Mike.  They 
played duets featuring The Woodpecker Song, 
Domino and Chitarra Romana.  Then it was break 
time and the raffle. 
 
 
Always ensuring us a bountiful harvest of beautiful music at just the perfect time to fully enjoy it Mike Ma-
rotta (accordionist), Dave Dally (violinist) and Steve Hanson (string bassist) and  Oracio Aiello (tenor) were 
our featured performers.   Among their international garden offerings were musical selections from France (La 
Vie en Rose, L'hymne à L'amour, Non Je Ne Regrette Rien).  A baker by trade, the incomparable, operatically 
talented tenor, Oracio Aiello, brought us La Marseillaise, the national anthem of France.  C’est magnifique, 
Oracio! Our international garden was sprinkled with songs from around the world.  You Raise Me Up com-
posed by the Irish-Norwegian duo, Secret Garden, again featured Oracio.  We weren’t far from Kensington Gar-
dens, England when we heard several Beatles’ hits.  Spanish heat and gypsy passion were brought to the stage 
with Habanero, from Bizet’s opera, Carmen.  From Spain a selection of Espana Waltzes.  Our tour du monde 
continued with Volare, Delilah and the famous Neapolitan tune Funiculì, Funicula (with Scott Stanfield invited 
to provide bongo accompaniment!).  The group closed out their performance with Sabre Dance, a movement in 
the final act of Aram Khachaturian's ballet “Gayane”.  We could almost feel the sabres whishing by us.  What 
skill and talent!  You can hear more from these talented musicians on Thursday evenings at Lugano’s Swiss 
Bistro located at located 3670 The Barnyard, Carmel-By-The-Sea. 
We have long turned to music and gardens for sanctuary from the frenzy and tumult that surrounds us.  But, as 
we well know, both live music and summer gardens stand as restorative, nourishing, necessary havens.  Talk to 
me to hear more about summer gardens! Happy and safe summer to you!

Saturday, August 18 San Jose Giants game (the Junior team for the SF Giants.)  They will also play Take Me

S2E19: Advice Before Money: The VC Model Founders Want — With Mike Ma.
Startups Decoded - presented by Morrison Foerster - MoFo.com
Andy Walsh
Jan 19, 2026

Transcript
Mike Ma doesn’t invest in decks. He invests in people.
As Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, Mike works with what he calls “coachable superheroes”, early-stage, mission-driven founders tackling real problems in economic mobility, healthcare, climate, and education.
In this conversation, we unpack what it actually means to be coachable as a founder, why most advice fails in practice, and how real progress happens when coaching, capital, and execution collide. Mike shares lessons from the trenches — blending Fortune 500 experience with venture-backed CXO roles, and explains why the best founders don’t just seek answers, they build judgement.
We also explore Sidecut’s hands-on approach to venture building, the parallels between adaptive sports coaching and startup leadership, and why helping founders unlock potential often means meeting them exactly where they are, not where the pitch says they should be.
This episode is for founders who want fewer platitudes, better questions, and support that actually shows up.

Mike Ma
Managing Partner and Head Coach at Sidecut Ventures, where he invests in and coaches early-stage, mission-driven founders working on some of society’s hardest problems.
He brings a rare blend of Fortune 500 experience (Bank of America, Vanguard) and venture-backed CXO leadership(including Betterment and Own Up), rolling up his sleeves across product, strategy, and fundraising. Mike believes the best venture outcomes are built through proximity, trust, and real coaching, not performative advice.
Outside startups, Mike is an adaptive snowsports instructor and a former member of PSIA-AASI’s National Adaptive Team, training instructors to teach individuals of all abilities. The same coaching mindset he brings to the slopes, patience, adaptability, and belief in latent potential, underpins his work with founders.

Ep#86: Early Decisions That Define Your Startup Forever. With J.P. Morgan Asset Management.
Live podcast event with J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Girl Math Capital, and The Fourth Effect.
Andy Walsh
Sep 14, 2026
4
1
Share
Transcript
The big idea
Nobody sits a first-time founder down and tells them that incorporating alone creates a legal board, whether they’ve thought about it or not. Nobody tells them that a small check from an angel can come with a request for a board seat they didn’t need to give away. Nobody tells them that the safe they’re so relieved to close comes with almost no strings, right up until the priced round, when every string shows up at once.
I learned this the hard way, twice. Both my exits taught me the same lesson: the people advising you in year one usually haven’t made these calls before either. So I brought together a J.P. Morgan Asset Management advisor, an early-stage investor from Girl Math Capital, and a governance lawyer from The Fourth Effect in one room, in front of 60+ founders, and asked them to lay out exactly what happens before anyone tells you it’s happening. Board composition, deal terms, and what to do with the cash once it lands.
The single biggest takeaway: the decisions that feel small and procedural in month one are the ones that decide how much control you actually have by Series A.
Listen & Watch: Apple || Spotify || YouTube
Presented by J.P. Morgan
Helping venture-backed founders navigate the financial decisions that come after the term sheet. From capital preservation to liquidity strategy, we help companies make the most of every dollar they raise.
The constraint and filter question
The friction point is this: founders don’t know which early decisions are permanent until they’ve already made them.
Ask yourself right now: who is legally on your board, and can you name one decision they’ve formally ratified in the last quarter? If you can’t answer that cleanly, you’re exposed.
The framework
Here’s how the board actually evolves, whether you plan it or not. At incorporation, you and your co-founder are the board by default. No fundraise needed, no paperwork beyond the entity itself. At seed, if an investor writes a big enough check, usually somewhere between 10 and 20 percent of the fully diluted company, they can negotiate a board seat that comes with real fiduciary weight, not just a friendly check-in. At Series A, a third kind of seat shows up: the independent director, someone without a stake in either the founder’s or the investor’s agenda.
The mistake almost every first-time founder makes is doing nothing about the board until the investor director is already negotiated into the term sheet. By then, you’ve lost the leverage to choose who sits in the independent seat, and the room can tilt against you fast if there’s only one founder director across the table from one investor director. The fix is proactive, not reactive. Seed or seed-plus is the moment to start seating your own independent, before you’re forced to accept whoever the lead VC recommends. If you’re not ready for that, promote a trusted advisor to observer status first. They sit in the room, they don’t vote, and you keep control of who eventually earns the real seat.
The same logic runs through fundraising structure and cash management. A SAFE gives you almost total freedom because the investor has almost no formal claim on your decisions. A priced round changes that instantly, because now there’s a class of preferred stock with real shareholder rights attached, whether or not the investor takes a board seat. And once the money is actually in your account, the framework simplifies to three priorities in order: preserve the principal, keep it liquid enough to access when you need it, and only then think about yield. Founders who skip straight to yield, chasing an extra half point of return on money they’ll need in ninety days, are optimizing the wrong variable.
“Something that takes you five minutes now can save you eight hours in the future, if not more.”
The data
Founders retain voting control in 71% of companies post-Series A, down from 88% at seed, according to First Round Capital’s analysis of over 300 portfolio companies (PitchBook, Q4 2024, n=1,204 Series A rounds).
The typical board structure moves from three seats at seed (two founders, one investor) to five at Series A (two founders, two investors, one independent), and can flip to investor-majority by Series B.
34% of co-founder disputes that ended in a founder exit were preceded by an equal equity split at incorporation, compared to 19% for unequal splits, per First Round Capital’s 2024 founder survey.
Lead investors typically negotiate a board seat only when their check represents 10 to 20% of the fully diluted company. Smaller checks are increasingly offered observer rights instead, a compromise that preserves founder control without shutting out valuable investors.
Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) can shield founders from significant capital gains tax at exit, but moving too much post-raise cash into non-qualifying investment vehicles can jeopardize that exemption entirely, a detail that rarely comes up until it’s too late to fix.
The playbook
Run this sequence before you’re forced into any of it by a term sheet:
Incorporation. Confirm who is legally a director today. Write down every material decision you’re already making.
Pre-seed to seed. Choose one or two trusted advisors and formalize observer rights before you need to fill a real seat.
Seed to seed-plus. If you’re not seating an independent yet, get directors and officers insurance in place. If a carrier will underwrite you, you’re ready.
Before any priced round. Get a clean cap table, historical and projected financials, and a use-of-funds narrative that answers two questions: why are you burning what you’re burning, and what milestone does this raise actually buy you?
After the round closes. Split cash into three buckets by timeline: three to six months of burn in checking and savings, the next stretch in a money market fund, and nothing chasing yield that you’ll need before it matures.
The worksheet
Before your next fundraising conversation, answer these on paper:
Who is currently on my board, and have we documented a single decision this quarter?
If my lead investor asked for a board seat tomorrow, do I know what percentage triggers that request, and am I prepared to negotiate it?
Do I have one advisor I trust enough to give observer rights to before I need an independent director?
Can I state, in one sentence, why I’m burning what I’m burning and what this raise gets me?
If the round closed today, do I know exactly which bucket, checking, savings, or money market, each dollar goes into?
The operating rule
The decisions that feel too small to matter in month one are the ones deciding how much control you have by Series A.
